name: Fitness Story DE
_comment_group: Another show under the Snapchat heading, cut to Hall of Femme's
design. Everything that makes it a Snapchat pack — the frame fetch,
the vertical output, the transcription, the rewrite, the card the
caption is set on — is Hall of Femme's and is stated in the same
numbers. What makes it a different show is the two things that are
visible from across a room: the face the words are set in, and the
colours they are set in.
Written as its own folder rather than as an override of
fitness-story, for the reason content/README.md gives: a channel is
a folder that gets dropped in. The prose below therefore points at
hall-of-femme wherever the reasoning is the same, and states its own
only where this pack actually decides something.
One thing this pack checked that its siblings had no reason to.
Acumin Pro's two files carry 626 codepoints each and cover the
umlauts, the eszett and the low quotes German sets speech in, so a
caption is drawn from the file rather than from whatever the browser
substitutes for a missing glyph — which would be a different face,
at a width nothing measured. Worth stating because a face chosen for
how it looks in English is not automatically a face that can SET
another language, and the check is two minutes against a cmap.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 vertical output, the transcription,
and the rewrite that turns the transcript from speech into reported
Stated as a reference and not as numbers, because this channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not — and a
pack that restates a shared answer is a pack that can be missing a
piece of it. That is not hypothetical: channels arrived under this
heading captioning their frames with the transcript as spoken,
because the folder they were copied from predated `rewrite`.
_comment_framing: How the frames are chosen and cropped, from
content/presets/snapchat-framing.json: the picture is the product,
so it is fitted to the canvas centred and left alone, and no frame
is rejected for failing to leave a column beside the subject that
this channel never sets anything in.
_comment_title: The whole of the difference between this show and its siblings.
Hall of Femme sets its captions in Telegraf — a 200-weight hairline
for the block, the 800 for a picked word — on a hot pink card.
Fitness Story sets them in HK Grotesk Italic on an electric blue
one. This pack sets them in Acumin Pro, upright, on a card that is
either plain white or plain black and is never anything else.
Three things follow, and all three are worth stating because they
are what a reader coming from one of the sibling packs will be
looking for.
The first is that there is no brand colour here, and that is the
design rather than a gap in it. Every other pack under this heading
puts its show's colour on the card, because the card is a fifth of
the frame and reads before anything set on it. This one has two
absolutes and the card is one of them, so what identifies the show
is not a hue at all — it is the maximum contrast a screen can draw,
which is the one thing a two-colour palette buys and the one thing
a coloured card can never quite have.
The second is that the face is doing more work than it does next
door. A hot pink card is recognisable at a glance whatever is set on
it; a white card is not, so Acumin has to be the difference. It is a
neo-grotesque — Akzidenz bones, large x-height, flat terminals — and
upright, which puts this pack between the two Open Sans shows
(upright block, slanted highlight) and Fitness Story (slanted
throughout). Set in black on white at 40px capitals it reads as
plain rather than as styled, which is the register this show is in.
The third is the highlight, and it is the one to argue with. Hall of
Femme spends 200 against 800 and Fitness Story 250 against 800 —
both of them the two ends of a weight axis, which at caption size is
as loud as a box would be. Acumin Pro is carried here in two cuts
and they are the Regular and the Bold, so this pack spends 400
against 700. That is the narrowest gap under the heading: a real
difference, and not a dramatic one.
It is also the only one available, which is why it is stated rather
than apologised for. The palette rules out a colour change, the
block is already upright so there is no slant left to spend, and the
preset's highlight mode is colour rather than box because the words
are already on a solid ground of their own. Widening it means a
third cut of Acumin in fonts/ and a face pack beside it; nothing
else here would have to change.
Everything else — the size, where the lines break, the capitals, the
shape of the card, where it stands on the frame, what a picked word
does — is the Snapchat caption design and is stated once, in
content/presets/snapchat-caption.json.

_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set
in until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of
its own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to
(see state.textColorFor). It is one of the two in `colors` below,
so the black swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an
untouched frame — the swatch is found by matching this value
rather than by being listed first.
Black letters on the white card is what the tool opens on, and
unlike its siblings' opening pairings there is nothing to weigh
up: it is the highest contrast of the four combinations this
palette allows, and the one a reader's eye is most practised at.
Absolute black, and the exact value matters. The card is a flat
shape rather than a photograph seen through it, so there is
nothing here for a true black to be too harsh against — and a
#111 that reads as black on a monitor turns into a grey slab
beside a genuinely black picture on a phone.
_comment_colors: The two colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and
for the card behind them — two buttons each in the title panel
(see editor.renderColorButtons). Nothing counts the entries: the
panel draws a swatch per colour and the row wraps, so a list of
two is as valid as hall-of-femme's four.
The same two in both lists, for the reason hall-of-femme states
at length: the point is the PAIRING rather than either colour.
Here that argument comes out smaller and sharper. Four
combinations instead of sixteen, of which two are the show —
black on white and white on black — and two are invisible.
Which is the honest cost of this palette and is worth naming.
Hall of Femme's answer to a user setting white on white is that
they can see it is invisible and press another swatch, and that
answer holds when a quarter of the grid is affected. Half of it
is a different proposition, and the reason the two lists are
still independent is that the alternative is worse: a rule
barring a matching pair would mean pressing white for the text
silently moved the card to black, so a user who wanted white on
black and pressed the two buttons in the other order would watch
the tool undo their first press. A palette of two colours that
can only be used one way round is not a palette, it is a
checkbox — and inverting a frame is exactly what this show's two
swatches are for.
White first in both rows, so the two rows read as the same
palette twice and the order matches the card an untouched frame
wears rather than the type on it. Neither list decides what that
is; `color` above and `panel.fill` below are the only place the
opening look is stated.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block — see the note
on `colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a
different CUT of the face and not a different colour, so what
colour the type is has one answer and not two.
_comment_highlight: Word scope, colour mode and what a second face costs are the
preset's — see snapchat-caption.json, which explains all three.
What this pack states is the two things that are its own: the
face a picked word changes to, and the colour it keeps.
The face is Acumin Pro Bold, 700 against the block's 400. Why
that is the whole of the emphasis available here, and how narrow
a gap it is next to the siblings, is argued in `_comment_title`
above rather than twice.
The colour is the block's, so the recolour draws a picked word
in exactly what its neighbours are drawn in and the weight is
the whole of the difference. Stated all the same, for the
fallback reason `color` above is stated — a highlight that
changed colour as well as weight would be two highlights, and
with two colours it would also be the only other thing the
palette can say.
The Bold is WIDER than the Regular, the same way round as the
pair fitness-story picks its words out with, and it is the one
consequence to know about.
Measured at 40px across a caption's worth of strings it runs 2.9%
to 4.3% wider — five pixels on a single word, fifteen on a line
of twenty-three characters. Lines are wrapped in the BLOCK's face
and nothing re-wraps them when a word is picked out afterwards
(see `measuredWidth` in js/text.js, which measures in the
selected channel's face, and `captionLines` in js/caption.js,
which runs once as the frames land), so a line already sitting at
the 90% width target can end up a few pixels past it, and the box
behind it — cut to its own line, see `panel` — steps out by the
same. It is small enough not to read as the graphic changing
shape, and the block is a text box the user rewraps by hand if it
ever does.
None of that would be small under a size FIT, which would resize
the whole block to whatever the widest line needs and so retype
the caption around the word being emphasised. It is one of the
two reasons the preset's layout states its size instead.
_comment_panel: The card the caption is set on, in whichever of the two colours
the frame is wearing. Every number in it is hall-of-femme's, and
the long argument for each is there rather than repeated here:
one box per LINE and `joined`, so the background is a single
shape that steps in and out with the sentence instead of a
rectangle the width of its longest line; 12 of padding, which is
a highlighter's margin and not a card's; no border, because a
keyline would make the slab read as a box drawn over the picture
rather than as a card lying on it; 13 of corner radius, the
number every background under this heading is rounded by; and a
White, and that shadow is the reason the choice is worth a line
rather than none. It is half opaque and offset far enough to be
seen as a shadow rather than as a dirty edge precisely so that a
white slab thrown onto a white wall still reads as a card lying
on the picture — a case every pack under this heading has to
survive, and the only one where this pack's opening card meets it
